Pass
pȧs
v. (to go by, move on, or come to an end; rendering Hebrew 'abar, Greek parerchomai)
From French passer, Latin passus, a step. Scripture uses the word for two opposite movements — the world passing away under judgment, and the LORD passing over His people in mercy.

Biblical Definition

To pass is to move by and be gone, and Scripture applies it first to the world men treat as permanent: “the fashion of this world passeth away” (1 Corinthians 7:31). The Apostle's word is not substance but fashion — the shape, the arrangement, the going order of things — and it is already in motion. Our Lord fixes the contrast that gives the doctrine its comfort: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matthew 24:35). The most solid things a man can name are the passing ones, and the least visible thing, the word of Christ, is what stands. The same verb turns to mercy at the Passover, where the LORD passes by the houses marked with blood: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you” (Exodus 12:13). Judgment moves through the land and steps over a house, and the reason given is not the character of those inside but the blood outside. The word finally describes what conversion does to a man's past: “if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). What passes there is not memory but dominion.

Webster 1828 Definition

To move from one place to another; to go by; to elapse; to be transferred; to come to an end. Scripture's two great uses are the world's passing away under judgment and the LORD's passing over His people in mercy.

expand to see more

PASS, v.i. [Fr. passer; L. passus, a step.] To move, in almost any manner; to go; to proceed from one place to another.

2. To go by; to move by or beyond; as, the procession passed.

3. To elapse; to be spent; as, the time passes rapidly.

4. To go away; to depart; to vanish; to cease; as, the storm has passed.

5. To be transferred from one owner to another; as, an estate passes by deed.

PASS, v.t. To go by, beyond, over or through; to omit; to overlook; to transcend; as, to pass a house; to pass the bounds of reason.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 7:31 — "And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away."

Matthew 24:35 — "Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away."

Exodus 12:13 — "And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and the plague shall not be upon you to destroy you, when I smite the land of Egypt. to"

2 Corinthians 5:17 — "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."

Modern Corruption

The passing of this world is treated as a poetic sentiment rather than a coming fact, and “passing away” has become a euphemism that lets men speak of death without naming it or its judgment.

expand to see more

Modern speech has taken the Bible's solemn verb and made it a softener. A man no longer dies; he passes. The substitution looks like kindness and functions as evasion, because the word that Scripture uses to announce the end of the world is put to work hiding the end of a life. Where death cannot be named, judgment cannot be named either, and the comfort that Scripture actually offers — that the words of Christ do not pass away when heaven and earth do — is never reached. Plain speech about death is the doorway to real consolation, and euphemism bars it.

The deeper corruption is practical rather than verbal: living as though the fashion of this world were the durable thing. The Apostle wrote 1 Corinthians 7:31 to men buying, marrying, and using the world, and he did not forbid these things; he relativized them by a fact. What passes is to be used and not leaned upon. Recover the ordering — heaven and earth pass, His word does not; the plague passes over the blood-marked house; old things are passed away in Christ — and the word stops being a euphemism and becomes a discipline.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'abar (to pass over, through, or by) is the verb of crossing Jordan and of the Passover itself; Greek parerchomai (to pass by, pass away) carries the eschatological sense in our Lord's words.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'abar (H5674) — to pass over, through, or by; used of crossing rivers, of transgressing a command, and of the LORD passing before Moses.

Hebrew pacach (H6452) — to pass over, to spare; the verb behind pesach, the Passover, in Exodus 12:13.

Greek parerchomai (G3928) — to pass by, to pass away; the word of Matthew 24:35 for heaven and earth.

Greek paragō (G3855) — to lead past, to pass away; used of the world and its fashion going by.

Greek schēma (G4976) — fashion, outward form; the precise thing Paul says is passing in 1 Corinthians 7:31.

Usage

"“The fashion of this world passeth away” — the arrangement of things is temporary, not the creation itself."

"“My words shall not pass away” — the permanence men assign to heaven and earth belongs to Christ's speech."

"“I will pass over you” — judgment steps over a house on account of blood."
